3.2.5.5-f1.accuracy_reason: In medieval medical writers such as Guainerius, 'heros' means the sufferer from amor hereos/heroicus, that is, the lover.

3.2.5.5-f10.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 6.129 reads 'hoc opus, hic labor est'.

3.2.5.5-f102.accuracy_reason: Papinian was the Roman jurist and Paul the apostle. The sentence is Jerome's Letter 77.

3.2.5.5-f107.accuracy_reason: Dio 56.1–10 records Augustus speaking separately to the unmarried and married equites (AD 9), and Burton's sidenote cites the same book. 'Rome' is indeed English.

3.2.5.5-f112.accuracy_reason: This is a correct description of the Roman ius trium liberorum.

3.2.5.5-f113.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.28 has 'sponsi Penelopae'. 'Penelopes' is a Greek genitive.

3.2.5.5-f116.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Phaedra 461, comes from the Nurse's speech to Hippolytus.

3.2.5.5-f119.accuracy_reason: This is Hippolytus' outburst against women in Seneca's Phaedra (about line 566).

3.2.5.5-f127.accuracy_reason: Philippus Beroaldus the elder married Camilla, daughter of the jurist Vincenzo Paleotti, and the gloss of 'ex animi sententia' is fair.

3.2.5.5-f136.accuracy_reason: The Latin renders Odysseus' words to Nausicaa (Odyssey 6.182–4) about husband and wife living of one mind, so 'Latin Homer' as Homer in a Latin version is right.

3.2.5.5-f14.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.284 reads 'quae prima exordia sumat?', of Aeneas wondering how to approach Dido.

3.2.5.5-f168.accuracy_reason: In Seneca's Phaedra the Nurse urges Hippolytus with these lines to give up his chaste, solitary life.

3.2.5.5-f169.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 1.9.17, has 'donec virenti canities abest morosa', and Burton's 'viventi' departs from it.

3.2.5.5-f17.accuracy_reason: Moschus' Idyll 6 is the chain Pan–Echo–Satyr–Lyde and closes on this thought of mutual hatred.

3.2.5.5-f172.accuracy_reason: Valerius Maximus (7.2 ext. 1) records Socrates' answer that a man will repent whether he marries or not.

3.2.5.5-f179.accuracy_reason: In Ovid, Metamorphoses 9, Iphis, a girl raised as a boy, is turned into a man (by Isis) so she can marry Ianthe.

3.2.5.5-f183.accuracy_reason: The refrain 'Hymen o Hymenaee, Hymen ades o Hymenaee' is that of Catullus 62.

3.2.5.5-f185.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 5.56: Aeneas says this on landing again in Sicily at Anchises' tomb.

3.2.5.5-f187.accuracy_reason: The lines come from Catullus 61 (about lines 204–5), near the end of the epithalamium for Manlius and Junia (or Vinia), and Burton's English adds the details the note mentions.

3.2.5.5-f189.accuracy_reason: The Historia Augusta (Gallieni duo 11.8) preserves Gallienus' epithalamium with these lines. Burton's 'O juvenes' differs from the text's 'o pueri', but the note doesn't claim otherwise. Burton's English does say 'oyster kissings'.

3.2.5.5-f190.accuracy_reason: Theocritus, Idyll 18 (the Epithalamium of Helen) has Ζεὺς Κρονίδας granting lasting wealth. The note rightly hedges the Saturnus explanation with 'probably'.

3.2.5.5-f192.accuracy_reason: Ovid Met. 8.708–710 is Philemon's first-person prayer, quoted correctly, and Burton does recast it in the third person.

3.2.5.5-f193.accuracy_reason: These are Aen. 9.446–447 on Nisus and Euryalus, and the sidenote Ovid Met. 8 does refer to the preceding lines.

3.2.5.5-f215.accuracy_reason: Genius as natural appetite or inclination ('indulgere genio') is the right sense here.

3.2.5.5-f217.accuracy_reason: Heauton Timorumenos 213–216 is Clitipho's complaint about 'iniqui patres … a pueris ilico nasci senes', which Burton quotes.

3.2.5.5-f22.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Ecl. 2.19 is Corydon addressing Alexis.

3.2.5.5-f237.accuracy_reason: Georgics 3.284 reads 'fugit inreparabile tempus', so the phrase is an echo, as the note says.

3.2.5.5-f240.accuracy_reason: Theocritus, Idyll 12.15–16 has the golden men of old, when the one loved loved back.

3.2.5.5-f252.accuracy_reason: The line is Horace, Sat. 1.1.68, 'Tantalus a labris sitiens fugientia captat flumina'. The note doesn't give the locus, but what it says is right.

3.2.5.5-f265.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Cons. 3 pr. 7 cites Euripides (Andromache) saying the childless man is 'infortunio felix'. Burton's gloss does reverse the paradox.

3.2.5.5-f28.accuracy_reason: Met. 1.478–480 reads 'aversata' and has line 479 ('inpatiens expersque viri…') between the two lines Burton quotes.

3.2.5.5-f286.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Eclogue 2.56 reads 'Rusticus es, Corydon; nec munera curat Alexis', with Corydon addressing himself; Burton's 'est' makes it third person.

3.2.5.5-f287.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.426 is said of Narcissus and his reflection; Burton's 'he dotes, is doted on again' applies it to a pair of lovers.

3.2.5.5-f295.accuracy_reason: 'Native' (natus) is indeed the astrological term for the subject of a nativity.

3.2.5.5-f298.accuracy_reason: The palinode is Stesichorus' recantation about Helen. Burton is quoting Philippus Beroaldus, who married Camilla Paleotti, as the sidenote shows.

3.2.5.5-f309.accuracy_reason: 'Resolutions upon a question' are horary judgements, and whether one will win a mistress is a standard horary question.

3.2.5.5-f313.accuracy_reason: The seventh house is the house of marriage, the second governs wealth, and the twelfth governs servitude, imprisonment and secret enemies. That is standard astrological doctrine.

3.2.5.5-f33.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.438–39 reads 'sed nullis ille movetur / fletibus…' and is about Aeneas; Burton's 'illa' makes it feminine, and his English couplet is indeed a free generalization.

3.2.5.5-f35.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.353–55 reads 'cupiere', 'dura' and 'tetigere'. The note's account of Burton's variants and their effect is correct.

3.2.5.5-f4.accuracy_reason: Burton plays on phlebotomy (opening a vein, here for a pleurisy) and Hymen, the god of marriage.

3.2.5.5-f42.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 1.7.27: 'nil desperandum Teucro duce et auspice Teucro'.

3.2.5.5-f44.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Ars Amatoria 1.669–70 continues 'si non et cetera sumpsit, / haec quoque quae data sunt perdere dignus erit', as the note paraphrases.

3.2.5.5-f46.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 12.937 reads 'tua est Lavinia coniunx', spoken by the defeated Turnus; Burton's subjunctive 'sit' changes the force.

3.2.5.5-f49.accuracy_reason: Heauton Timorumenos 213 (Clitipho) does read 'quam iniqui sunt patres in omnis adulescentis iudices', and Burton's sidenote 'Ter.' matches.

3.2.5.5-f55.accuracy_reason: At the end of the Heauton Timorumenos, Clitipho turns down the red-haired girl his father offers and asks for Archonides' daughter instead. The note describes this and Burton's use of it correctly.

3.2.5.5-f59.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 9.32–33 reads 'fatum est et partibus illis / quas sinus abscondit', and it does refer to the private parts. The note reports Burton's change of 'et' to 'in' correctly.

3.2.5.5-f70.accuracy_reason: These are the closing lines of the Ausonian 'De rosis nascentibus' (Idyll 14), where a rose blooms at dawn and has faded by evening. Eous is the Morning Star.

3.2.5.5-f72.accuracy_reason: The line is Ovid, Ars Amatoria 2.669, and it continues 'tolerate labores' as the note says. But in Ovid the 'labores' are already the work of love, in praise of older mistresses. So 'Burton applies it to love' wrongly suggests he changed its sense. The note also doesn't name the work.

3.2.5.5-f73.accuracy_reason: The lines are Catullus 5.4–6, and the standard text reads 'perpetua'. The English is from Jonson's song 'Come, my Celia' in Volpone, as Burton's sidenote says.

3.2.5.5-f76.accuracy_reason: This is Megadorus' speech in the Aulularia (about lines 478–482). The quotation does start partway through his sentence.

3.2.5.5-f79.accuracy_reason: In the usual story (Callimachus, Ovid Heroides 20–21), Cydippe reads the oath aloud and so binds herself to marry Acontius. The masculine forms in Burton's Latin do turn it into Acontius' own promise.

3.2.5.5-f83.accuracy_reason: Aelian, Varia Historia 13.33, does tell the story of Rhodopis' shoe and the eagle.

3.2.5.5-f92.accuracy_reason: The proverb appears in Terence, Phormio 506, and in Erasmus, Adagia I.v.25, and it means what the note says.

3.2.5.5-f93.accuracy_reason: 'Cornutum' (the horned argument, or dilemma) is a standard term in logic.

3.2.5.5-f94.accuracy_reason: The Arabic 'parts' (lots) of marriage and lust, and the triplicities, are described correctly. Calling 'triplicates' a probable corruption is properly hedged. 'Ruled by a planet' is a loose simplification but acceptable.

3.2.5.5-f97.accuracy_reason: Nepos, Atticus 11.6 has 'sui cuique mores fingunt fortunam'.
